content: Chest pain is a cardinal symptom requiring immediate evaluation. Causes range from life-threatening (myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection) to benign (musculoskeletal, gastroesophageal reflux). Cardiac chest pain is typically crushing, pressure-like, radiating to left arm or jaw, accompanied by diaphoresis and dyspnea. ST elevation on ECG indicates STEMI requiring immediate PCI. Troponin I/T are biomarkers of myocardial injury; elevated levels confirm acute MI. Unstable angina presents with rest pain or crescendo pattern without troponin rise. Management: aspirin 325mg, oxygen if SpO2 <94%, nitrates (avoid if systolic BP <90), morphine for refractory pain, and urgent cardiology referral. Pulmonary embolism causes pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and hemoptysis; D-dimer screening followed by CT pulmonary angiography. Aortic dissection presents with tearing pain radiating to the back; CT angiography is diagnostic.

Fever is defined as body temperature above 38.0°C (100.4°F). It is a regulated physiological response mediated by prostaglandin E2 acting on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory centre. Common causes: viral infections (influenza, COVID-19, dengue), bacterial infections (pneumonia, UTI, sepsis), non-infectious causes (malignancy, autoimmune disease, drug fever). High fever above 39.5°C may cause febrile seizures in children. Hyperpyrexia (>41°C) is a medical emergency. Evaluation includes CBC, blood cultures x2, urinalysis, and chest X-ray. Neutrophilia with band forms suggests bacterial infection; lymphocytosis suggests viral etiology. Management: paracetamol 500–1000mg every 4–6 hours (max 4g/day), NSAIDs (ibuprofen), adequate hydration. Cold sponging is no longer recommended. Dengue fever: monitor platelet count daily; platelet <20,000 or bleeding requires hospitalization.

Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by hyperglycemia. Type 1 DM: autoimmune destruction of beta cells, absolute insulin deficiency, onset in youth, DKA prone. Type 2 DM: insulin resistance + progressive beta-cell failure, accounts for 90% of cases. Diagnostic criteria: fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL, HbA1c ≥6.5%, random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms, or 2-hr OGTT glucose ≥200 mg/dL. HbA1c target: <7% for most patients, <8% for elderly. Microvascular complications: retinopathy (annual eye exam), nephropathy (monitor urine albumin/creatinine ratio), neuropathy (10g monofilament foot exam). Macrovascular: MI, stroke, peripheral arterial disease. Management: lifestyle modification (diet, exercise), Metformin first-line for T2DM, GLP-1 agonists/SGLT-2 inhibitors if CVD risk. Hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL): 15g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes. DKA: glucose >250, ketones, bicarbonate <18, pH <7.3 — requires IV fluids, insulin infusion, potassium replacement.

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is defined as sustained BP ≥130/80 mmHg (AHA/ACC 2017) or ≥140/90 mmHg (JNC 7 / many international guidelines). Stage 1: 130–139/80–89; Stage 2: ≥140/90; Hypertensive urgency: ≥180/110 without end-organ damage; Hypertensive emergency: severe elevation with end-organ damage (stroke, MI, AKI, papilledema). Primary (essential) hypertension accounts for 90–95% of cases; secondary causes include renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, and obstructive sleep apnea. Target organ damage: LV hypertrophy, proteinuria, CKD, retinal changes, carotid intima-media thickening. First-line medications: thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, calcium channel blockers. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred in diabetic nephropathy. Beta-blockers for concurrent ischemic heart disease. Lifestyle modifications: DASH diet, sodium restriction (<2g/day), regular aerobic exercise, weight loss, smoking cessation, limit alcohol.

Stroke is a sudden neurological deficit from cerebrovascular cause. Ischemic stroke (85%): thrombotic or embolic occlusion. Hemorrhagic stroke (15%): intracerebral or subarachnoid hemorrhage. FAST acronym: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency. Golden hour: IV tPA (alteplase) within 4.5 hours of symptom onset for ischemic stroke without contraindications; mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 hours for large vessel occlusion. CT head without contrast: rules out hemorrhage before thrombolysis. NIHSS score quantifies deficit severity. Risk factors: hypertension (most important), atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, hyperlipidemia, prior TIA. TIA: transient symptoms <24 hours (usually <1 hour), high risk of stroke within 48 hours; same-day evaluation with ABCD2 score, MRI diffusion, carotid ultrasound. Secondary prevention: antiplatelet agents (aspirin + clopidogrel short-term), statins, BP control. Anticoagulation for cardioembolic (AF-related) stroke.

Dyspnea (shortness of breath) is the subjective sensation of breathing difficulty. Acute causes: pneumonia, acute asthma exacerbation, COPD exacerbation, pulmonary edema (acute heart failure), pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, anaphylaxis. Chronic causes: COPD, asthma, heart failure, ILD, pulmonary hypertension, obesity hypoventilation, anemia. Key assessment: onset, duration, associated symptoms (chest pain, cough, fever, orthopnea, PND, leg swelling), triggers, oxygen saturation. Emergency red flags: SpO2 <90%, respiratory rate >30/min, use of accessory muscles, altered consciousness. Investigations: pulse oximetry, ABG, CXR, CBC, BNP (heart failure), D-dimer (PE). BNP >500 pg/mL strongly suggests heart failure. Treatment: supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 94–98%, bronchodilators for asthma/COPD, diuretics (furosemide) for pulmonary edema, anticoagulation for PE.

Dizziness encompasses vertigo (illusion of movement), presyncope (near-fainting), dysequilibrium (imbalance), and non-specific dizziness. BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo): most common cause, brief episodes triggered by head position change, positive Dix-Hallpike test, treated with Epley maneuver. Vestibular neuritis: acute severe vertigo following viral illness, no hearing loss, treated with vestibular suppressants. Meniere's disease: episodic vertigo + tinnitus + low-frequency hearing loss, treated with low-salt diet and diuretics. Central vertigo (stroke, tumor): associated neurological signs, HINTS exam (Head Impulse-Nystagmus-Test of Skew) differentiates from peripheral. Presyncope: vasovagal syncope, orthostatic hypotension (BP drop ≥20 systolic or ≥10 diastolic on standing), cardiac arrhythmia (Holter monitor). Medications causing dizziness: antihypertensives, sedatives, anticonvulsants, aminoglycosides (ototoxic).

Abdominal pain location guides diagnosis: RUQ — cholecystitis, hepatitis, biliary colic; Epigastric — peptic ulcer, GERD, pancreatitis, MI (referred); LUQ — splenomegaly, gastric pathology; Periumbilical — early appendicitis, small bowel obstruction, AAA; RLQ — appendicitis, ovarian cyst/torsion, Crohn's disease, ectopic pregnancy; LLQ — diverticulitis, sigmoid volvulus, ovarian pathology; Diffuse — peritonitis, mesenteric ischemia, IBD. Acute abdomen (rigidity, rebound tenderness, guarding) is a surgical emergency. LFTs, lipase (pancreatitis >3× ULN diagnostic), CBC, CRP, urinalysis, βhCG in women of reproductive age. Appendicitis: Alvarado score, ultrasound, CT abdomen if uncertain; McBurney's point tenderness. Cholecystitis: Murphy's sign, right upper quadrant ultrasound showing gallbladder wall thickening >3mm and pericholecystic fluid. NSAIDs for renal/biliary colic; IV fluids, NBM for surgical conditions. Red flags: weight loss, dysphagia, rectal bleeding, family history of GI cancer.

Headache classification: Primary (migraine, tension-type, cluster) and Secondary (SAH, meningitis, hypertensive crisis, space-occupying lesion). Red flag headaches (SNOOP4): Systemic symptoms, Neurological signs, Onset sudden ('thunderclap'), Older age onset >50, Progressive worsening, Postural component, Precipitated by Valsalva, Papilledema. Thunderclap headache (worst headache of life, maximal in seconds) requires emergency CT head, then LP if CT negative (xanthochromia for SAH). Migraine: unilateral throbbing, moderate–severe, nausea/vomiting, photophobia/phonophobia, lasting 4–72 hours, worsened by activity; treat with triptans, NSAIDs. Cluster headache: strictly unilateral orbital/periorbital pain, autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, ptosis), attacks 15–180 min, cluster periods weeks–months; treat with 100% O2, subcutaneous sumatriptan. Tension-type: bilateral pressing/tightening, mild–moderate, no nausea; treat with simple analgesics, avoid overuse. Chronic daily headache: >15 headache-days/month; medication overuse is common trigger.

Anemia is defined as hemoglobin below normal (<13 g/dL in men, <12 g/dL in women, <11 g/dL in pregnancy). Classification by MCV: microcytic (<80 fL) — iron deficiency, thalassemia, sideroblastic; normocytic (80–100 fL) — anemia of chronic disease, aplastic anemia, hemolysis, acute blood loss; macrocytic (>100 fL) — folate/B12 deficiency, liver disease, hypothyroidism. Iron deficiency anemia: most common worldwide, causes: blood loss (GI, menstrual), poor intake, malabsorption; low serum iron, high TIBC, low ferritin (<12 μg/L diagnostic); treat with ferrous sulfate 325mg TID for 3–6 months. Vitamin B12 deficiency: subacute combined degeneration of cord (posterior and lateral columns), glossitis, hypersegmented neutrophils; treat with IM cyanocobalamin or high-dose oral B12. Hemolytic anemia: elevated LDH, unconjugated bilirubin, reticulocytes, low haptoglobin; Coombs test for autoimmune hemolysis. Sickle cell anemia: HbSS; vaso-occlusive crisis treated with IV fluids, analgesics, oxygen; hydroxyurea reduces crisis frequency.

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined as GFR <60 mL/min/1.73m² or markers of kidney damage for >3 months. Staging: G1 (GFR≥90, markers of damage), G2 (60–89), G3a (45–59), G3b (30–44), G4 (15–29), G5 (<15, kidney failure). Causes: diabetic nephropathy (most common), hypertensive nephrosclerosis, glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney disease. Serum creatinine and eGFR (CKD-EPI formula) monitor progression. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR): normal <30, microalbuminuria 30–300, macroalbuminuria >300 mg/g. Complications: anemia (EPO deficiency), hyperphosphatemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, metabolic acidosis, fluid overload. ACE inhibitors/ARBs are renoprotective in diabetic and proteinuric CKD. Avoid NSAIDs and contrast agents in CKD. AKI: rapid rise in creatinine (≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 hrs or ≥50% in 7 days) or oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr for ≥6 hrs); causes: prerenal (volume depletion), intrinsic (ATN, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis), postrenal (obstruction).

Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is the most common cause of infection-related mortality. Typical organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common), Haemophilus influenzae. Atypical organisms: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila (associated with air conditioning, hyponatremia). Symptoms: fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea. Diagnosis: CXR (lobar/segmental consolidation), CBC (neutrophilia), sputum culture. CURB-65 score (Confusion, Urea >7, Respiratory rate ≥30, BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic, Age ≥65): 0–1 outpatient, 2 hospital, ≥3 ICU consideration. Antibiotic choice: outpatient — amoxicillin + azithromycin; inpatient — IV beta-lactam + macrolide or respiratory fluoroquinolone. COVID-19 pneumonia: bilateral ground-glass opacities on CT, pulse oximetry monitoring, remdesivir + dexamethasone for hospitalized patients. Influenza: Oseltamivir within 48 hours of onset, yearly vaccination recommended.

Heart failure (HF) is a clinical syndrome of dyspnea, fatigue, and fluid retention due to structural or functional cardiac abnormalities. HFrEF (reduced EF <40%): ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol), MRAs (spironolactone), SGLT-2 inhibitors; ICD if EF <35%. HFpEF (preserved EF ≥50%): mainly diuretics, BP/AF control, SGLT-2 inhibitors. NYHA Classification: I (no symptoms with ordinary activity), II (slight limitation), III (marked limitation), IV (symptoms at rest). Acute decompensated HF: pulmonary edema, orthopnea — IV furosemide, oxygen, IV nitrates if hypertensive, BiPAP if respiratory failure. BNP/NT-proBNP: excellent biomarkers for diagnosis and monitoring; BNP >100 pg/mL raises suspicion. Echocardiogram is the cornerstone investigation. Common precipitants: non-compliance with medications/sodium restriction, arrhythmia (AF), infection, ischemia, anaemia, NSAID use. Fluid restriction 1.5–2L/day; daily weighing (notify if >2 kg gain in 2 days).

Major depressive disorder (MDD): depressed mood or anhedonia most of the day, nearly every day for ≥2 weeks, plus ≥4 additional symptoms (sleep change, appetite change, fatigue, concentration difficulty, guilt/worthlessness, psychomotor changes, suicidal ideation). PHQ-9 score: 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 moderately severe, ≥20 severe. First-line pharmacotherapy: SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine); SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine). Adequate trial: therapeutic dose for 4–8 weeks. Psychotherapy: CBT is equally effective to medication for mild–moderate depression. Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD): excessive uncontrollable worry ≥6 months with ≥3 symptoms (restlessness, fatigue, concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance). GAD-7 ≥10 suggests clinically significant anxiety. Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected panic attacks with persistent concern about future attacks. SSRI/SNRI first-line for GAD and panic disorder; benzodiazepines short-term only. Refer to mental health specialist for moderate–severe symptoms, suicidal ideation, or treatment resistance.

COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) presents with fever, dry cough, dyspnea, fatigue, anosmia, ageusia, myalgia, sore throat, diarrhea. Incubation: 2–14 days (median 5 days). Severity: mild (no pneumonia), moderate (pneumonia, SpO2 ≥94%), severe (SpO2 <94%, RR >30), critical (ARDS, septic shock, organ failure). Diagnosis: RT-PCR nasopharyngeal swab (gold standard), rapid antigen test for screening. CXR/CT: bilateral ground-glass opacities, consolidation. Inflammatory markers: elevated CRP, ferritin, LDH, D-dimer indicate severe disease. Management: mild–moderate — supportive care, antigen tests, isolation 5 days. Severe — remdesivir (within 10 days), dexamethasone 6mg/day, prophylactic anticoagulation (enoxaparin). Long COVID: persistent symptoms >12 weeks — fatigue, brain fog, dyspnea, palpitations. Vaccination: primary series + boosters recommended for all eligible individuals. High-risk: age >60, obesity, DM, CKD, immunosuppression, cardiovascular disease.

Hypothyroidism: elevated TSH, low free T4. Causes: Hashimoto thyroiditis (most common; positive anti-TPO antibodies), post-radioiodine/post-surgery, iodine deficiency. Symptoms: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, bradycardia, dry skin, hair loss, depression, menstrual irregularity. Myxedema coma: severe hypothyroidism with altered consciousness — emergency. Treatment: levothyroxine (T4) starting low (25–50 mcg/day), titrate by TSH every 6–8 weeks; target TSH 0.5–2.5 mIJ/L. Hyperthyroidism: suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3. Causes: Graves' disease (autoimmune, diffuse goiter, exophthalmos), toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma. Symptoms: weight loss, palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, anxiety, diarrhea, AF. Thyroid storm: severe hyperthyroidism with hyperpyrexia, tachycardia, altered mental status — propylthiouracil + iodine + propranolol + steroids. Treatment options: antithyroid drugs (methimazole/propylthiouracil), radioiodine ablation, thyroidectomy. Subclinical hypothyroidism: elevated TSH with normal T4 — treat if TSH >10 or symptomatic.

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with variable airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Triggers: allergens, exercise, cold air, NSAIDs (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease), beta-blockers, viral URTI, emotional stress. Symptoms: recurrent wheezing, cough (especially nocturnal), chest tightness, dyspnea. Diagnosis: FEV1/FVC <70% on spirometry with ≥12% (and ≥200mL) bronchodilator reversibility. PEFR monitoring at home. Classification: intermittent (symptoms ≤2 days/week), mild persistent, moderate persistent, severe persistent. GINA step therapy: Step 1 — as-needed SABA; Step 2 — low-dose ICS; Step 3 — low-dose ICS + LABA; Step 4 — medium–high-dose ICS + LABA; Step 5 — add-on therapy (tiotropium, anti-IgE, anti-IL5). Acute severe asthma: PEFR <50%, SpO2 <90%, unable to complete sentences — salbutamol nebs, ipratropium, oral/IV prednisolone, oxygen. Life-threatening: silent chest, cyanosis, bradycardia, confusion — IV magnesium sulfate 2g, consider intubation.

Complete Blood Count (CBC): WBC 4–11 ×10⁹/L (neutrophilia bacterial infection, lymphocytosis viral, eosinophilia allergy/parasites), RBC 4.5–5.5 (men)/4.0–5.0 (women) ×10¹²/L, Hemoglobin 13–17 (men)/12–16 (women) g/dL, Hematocrit 40–52% (men)/36–48% (women), MCV 80–100 fL, Platelets 150–400 ×10⁹/L. Metabolic/Chemistry: Sodium 136–145, Potassium 3.5–5.0, Chloride 98–106, Bicarbonate 22–29 mEq/L, Glucose fasting 70–99 mg/dL (≥126 diagnostic of DM), Creatinine 0.6–1.2 (men)/0.5–1.1 (women) mg/dL, BUN 7–20 mg/dL, eGFR ≥60 normal. Liver: ALT 7–56 U/L, AST 10–40 U/L, ALP 44–147 U/L, Total bilirubin 0.1–1.2 mg/dL, Albumin 3.5–5.0 g/dL. Lipids: Total cholesterol <200 mg/dL, LDL <100 mg/dL (<70 high-risk), HDL >40 (men)/>50 (women) mg/dL, Triglycerides <150 mg/dL. Thyroid: TSH 0.4–4.0 mIU/L, Free T4 0.8–1.8 ng/dL. Cardiac: Troponin I <0.04 ng/mL, BNP <100 pg/mL, CK-MB 0–5 ng/mL. Coagulation: PT/INR 0.8–1.2, APTT 25–35 sec.

Analgesics: Paracetamol 500–1000mg every 4–6h (max 4g/day) first-line for mild–moderate pain; Ibuprofen 400mg every 6–8h with food; avoid NSAIDs in CKD, peptic ulcer, HF. Antibiotics: Amoxicillin 500mg TID for LRTI/URTI; Azithromycin 500mg day 1 then 250mg daily ×4 days (Z-pack); Ciprofloxacin 500mg BD for UTI/GI infections; Metronidazole for anaerobes/H.pylori. Hypertension: Amlodipine 5–10mg OD; Ramipril 2.5–10mg OD; Losartan 50–100mg OD; Bisoprolol 2.5–10mg OD. Diabetes: Metformin 500mg–1000mg BD with meals; reduce dose if eGFR 30–45, stop if <30; Metformin causes GI side effects, lactic acidosis risk. Respiratory: Salbutamol (Ventolin) 100–200mcg inhaler PRN; Seretide (fluticasone/salmeterol) ICS/LABA BD. Statins: Atorvastatin 20–80mg OD at night; monitor LFTs and CK for myopathy; avoid with grapefruit juice. Anticoagulants: Warfarin with regular INR monitoring (target 2–3); DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban) for AF/DVT without routine monitoring. Proton pump inhibitors: Omeprazole 20–40mg OD before meals for GERD/peptic ulcer.

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection. Sepsis Criteria (Sepsis-3): suspected infection + SOFA score increase ≥2. Quick SOFA (qSOFA): respiratory rate ≥22, altered mentation, systolic BP ≤100 — score ≥2 warrants concern. Septic shock: sepsis + vasopressors required to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg + serum lactate >2 mmol/L. Hour-1 Bundle: blood cultures ×2 before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥4, vasopressors (norepinephrine first-line) if MAP <65. Common sources: pneumonia, urosepsis, abdominal source, line infection, skin/soft tissue. Biomarkers: CRP, procalcitonin (PCT >2 ng/mL suggests bacterial sepsis, >10 ng/mL suggests severe sepsis/septic shock), lactate. Source control: drain abscesses, remove infected devices. Monitor: urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/hr, repeat lactate in 2 hours (clearance >10% is favorable), CBC, creatinine, coagulation (DIC), liver function. ICU admission for hemodynamic instability.

WHO analgesic ladder: Step 1 — non-opioids (paracetamol, NSAIDs, COX-2 inhibitors); Step 2 — weak opioids (tramadol, codeine) + non-opioids; Step 3 — strong opioids (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl) + non-opioids. NRS/VAS pain scale: 0 (no pain), 1–3 mild, 4–6 moderate, 7–10 severe. Neuropathic pain adjuvants: gabapentin 300–3600mg/day, pregabalin 75–300mg BD, amitriptyline 10–75mg nocte, duloxetine 60–120mg/day. Opioid side effects: constipation (always prescribe laxative), nausea (metoclopramide), respiratory depression (naloxone reversal), dependence. Opioid-induced constipation: polyethylene glycol, senna, methylnaltrexone for refractory cases. NSAIDs contraindications: CKD (eGFR <30), peptic ulcer disease, anticoagulation, third trimester pregnancy, HF. Multimodal analgesia optimizes pain control while minimizing individual drug side effects. Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) provides better pain control post-operatively.
source: WHO Pain Guidelines / Palliative Medicine Reference
